I'm 49, been farming these 7.8 mu for 30 years since my father handed me the hoe. My family has six people — my wife, my younger son, my daughter who's in middle school, and my aging parents. My eldest son works in a factory in Handan and sends back about 2,000 yuan a month, which helps with school fees and my father's medicine. But the farm has to carry its own weight. I split the land: 5 mu does wheat-maize double cropping, that's our grain and stability. The other 2.8 mu is cotton — cotton gives cash, and with the gin just 3 li down the road, I can sell it easy. I don't put everything in one basket; that's how you go hungry.

**Wheat** goes in around October 12th, when the soil still holds some warmth. I plant Jinmai 22, an improved variety. I save some seed but I bought fresh seed too — about 50 yuan per mu. The extension fellow at the township station says 15 kg nitrogen per mu, but my east plot is a bit sandy and last year the wheat turned yellow early, so I'm doing 17 kg N total. I put down compound fertilizer as base before planting, then topdress with urea at jointing in March if the crop looks like it needs it. I add phosphorus and potassium in the base too — the soil here's been mined for years. Irrigation is my biggest worry after the price of electricity went up. I'll irrigate three times: before winter freeze-up, at jointing, and at heading. Four would be ideal but the pumping bill would break me. I still remember 2019 — only twice, and I got barely 300 kg per mu. Never again. I spray herbicide before planting and watch for aphids in spring.

**Maize** has to go in fast after wheat harvest, usually June 8th to 10th. Sometimes I only have five days. I buy hybrid Zhengdan 958 seed fresh every year — 70 yuan per mu — saved seed doesn't vigor well for maize. I put compound fertilizer in the planting furrow, about 16 kg N equivalent. If we get good summer rains I might not topdress, but if it's dry at the 6-leaf stage I'll throw on some urea. Maize gets two irrigations: one around V8 and one at tasseling. Summer rains usually help, but you can't count on them. Me and my wife do most of the work, but for planting I hire three days of labor at 100 yuan per day — missing the window costs more than the wages. My daughter helps on weekends when school's out.

**Cotton** is planted mid-April, around the 15th. It's a fussy crop but the price has held steady. I use hybrid cotton seed, about 45 yuan per mu. Fertilizer is 14 kg N per mu — base at planting, then another shot at flowering. Cotton needs water at flowering and boll stage, so two irrigations. The real expense is pesticide — bollworm, aphids, spider mites. I spray four or five times with both insecticide and some fungicide, about 90 yuan per mu in chemicals. Skip a spray and you might as well not have planted. For picking in September and October, I hire three days of labor because cotton picking is back-breaking and my wife's wrists aren't what they used to be.

I'm looking at about 4,200 yuan in input costs this year. That's a lot of cash — after my father's hospital bill last winter, our savings are thin. I'm thinking of borrowing 1,000 yuan from my brother-in-law. But here's the thing: if I cut fertilizer or skip a pesticide spray to save money, I could lose half the crop. A bad year hurts more than a good year helps, so I'd rather apply a bit more than too little. I expect wheat around 420 kg per mu, maize around 470 kg per mu, and cotton lint around 230 kg per mu. If prices don't collapse, that should cover costs, pay back the loan, and leave enough for my daughter's school fees with a little buffer for emergencies.
